Hatim Chergui    Farhad Rezazadeh    Merouane Debbah Affiliation: and Christos Verikoukis,
Abstract

The path to higher network autonomy in 6G lies beyond the mere optimization of key performance indicators (KPIs). While KPIs have enabled automation gains under TM Forum Levels 1–3, they remain numerical abstractions that act only as proxies for the real essence of communication networks: seamless connectivity, fairness, adaptability, and resilience. True autonomy requires perceiving and reasoning over the network environment as it is. Such progress can be achieved through agentic AI, where large language model (LLM)-powered agents perceive multimodal telemetry, reason with memory, negotiate across domains, and act via APIs to achieve multi-objective goals. However, deploying such agents introduces the challenge of cognitive biases inherited from human design, which can distort reasoning, negotiation, tool use, and actuation. Between neuroscience and AI, this paper provides a tutorial on a selection of well-known biases, including their taxonomy, definition, mathematical formulation, emergence in telecom systems and the commonly impacted agentic components. The tutorial also presents various mitigation strategies tailored to each type of bias. The article finally provides two practical use-cases, which tackle the emergence, impact and mitigation gain of some famous biases in 6G inter-slice and cross-domain management. In particular, anchor randomization, temporal decay and inflection bonus techniques are introduced to specifically address anchoring, temporal and confirmation biases. This avoids that agents stick to the initial high resource allocation proposal or decisions that are recent and/or confirming a prior hypothesis. By grounding decisions in a richer and fairer set of past experiences, the quality and bravery of the agentic agreements in the second use-case, for instance, are leading to ×5\times 5 lower latency and around 40%40\% higher energy saving.

Index Terms:
6G, agentic AI, bias, network automation.

I Introduction

The landscape of telecom automation over the past 15 years can be structured along TM Forum’s maturity levels, from Level 1 (script-based) to Level 3 (analytics- and AI-assisted orchestration) [1], with initiatives such as 3GPP Self-Organizing Networks (SON), ETSI Zero-Touch Service Management (ZSM) and O-RAN. While their introduced paradigms have yielded operational efficiency, their optimization logic remains narrowly tethered to KPIs. However, those metrics are imperfect proxies/surrogates for the underlying objectives of communication systems. This reliance induces a well-documented failure mode captured by Goodhart’s Law, which states that “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure” [2]. In practice, this manifests as metric fixation [3], where algorithmic optimization maximizes numerical scores while neglecting harder-to-measure essence of the telecom environment and its users. In anticipation of 6G, overcoming this proxy-goal misalignment necessitates a transition from metric-centric optimization to goal-directed autonomy. This implies not only moving towards TM Forum Levels 4 and 5, but also embedding intelligence that can operate across dynamic, multi-domain, and partially observable environments. Agentic AI provides a viable paradigm: LLM-powered autonomous agents endowed with the ability to directly perceive through multimodal data (without proxies), reason over historical and contextual knowledge, plan adaptive courses of action, communicate under diverse intents, and act through APIs or network control functions. Crucially, such agents can negotiate across domains (e.g., RAN, edge, and core) to reconcile competing objectives, adapt to unforeseen conditions, and iteratively refine strategies via explanation and feedback. In this way, agentic AI would serve as the cognitive substrate for 6G networks, bridging the gap between low-level signals and high-level semantic goals. Rather than optimizing proxies, networks can pursue objectives that more faithfully represent the essence of telecommunication.

I-A Cognitive Biases in Agentic Systems

Special attention should be paid, however, to the susceptibility of agentic systems to the so-called cognitive biases, which are systematic deviations from rational judgment; a concept originally rooted in human psychology that agents could inherit in various ways and perpetuate, posing a tangible threat to the efficiency, fairness, and reliability of next-generation autonomous networks. Biases affect every layer of an agent’s behavior, from initial perception and reasoning to final decision-making and action execution. The foundational work on cognitive biases in human judgment was established by Tversky and Kahneman in their seminal paper, ”Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases” [4]. Their research demonstrated that humans rely on cognitive shortcuts, or heuristics, which can lead to predictable and systematic errors in judgment. In agentic systems, these biases are inherited and manifested across multiple layers. The insidious impact of biases can be observed throughout the entire agentic system pipeline, from perception to action. i) Prompts are a primary entry point for bias, where framing effects or the specific wording of instructions can skew an agent’s perception of a problem. For instance, prompting a network agent to “maximize throughput at all costs” can lead to a solution that ignores critical latency or fairness metrics. ii) Biases are deeply embedded in the training data, stemming from historical imbalances, cultural skews, and sampling errors. A large language model trained on data from a region with a specific network infrastructure could, when deployed elsewhere, exhibit a bias towards that legacy architecture, failing to optimally manage a new, more advanced one. Furthermore, biases emerge and compound in an agent’s internal processes, with implications for its reasoning and tool use. iii) The agent’s reasoning paths are susceptible to various heuristics. An agent tasked with dynamic resource allocation could exhibit an availability heuristic, disproportionately allocating bandwidth to a specific network slice from which it has received the most recent or frequent requests, thereby neglecting other slices in need. Similarly, a security agent may fall prey to a confirmation bias, only seeking out evidence that confirms a pre-existing threat model and overlooking a novel, unseen attack vector. These behaviors are akin to human shortcuts, where evidence is mis-weighted and readily accessible information is prioritized. iv) Biases are also evident in tool use, which includes the way memories are stored and retrieved, and how data sources and APIs are selected. An agent’s memory retrieval might be subject to recency/primacy biases, causing it to favor recently processed network logs over a more complete historical record, leading to short-sighted decisions. Conversely, an authority bias could lead an agent to show a strong, uncritical preference for data from a single, authoritative source or a familiar API, even when more suitable or diverse tools are available. The recent work by Xie et al. [5] highlights the growing concern of these biases, exploring their manifestation in large language models within multi-agent systems, a structure increasingly relevant to decentralized 6G architectures.

I-B Related Work

Drawing parallels with well-documented human biases such as confirmation bias, recency effects, and groupthink, recent research examines how similar distortions can manifest both within individual AI agents and across their interactions, potentially affecting collective decision-making, fairness, and safety. A comprehensive contribution in this domain is MindScope [6], which introduces a dataset encompassing 72 human cognitive biases and leverages it to evaluate how LLM agents display these distortions during multi-agent dialogue. Findings indicate that even when models appear well-aligned in isolation, their interactions can trigger latent, higher-order biases such as anchoring effects. Mitigation strategies—including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured debate mechanisms, and reinforcement learning (RL)-based adjudication—have shown promise in reducing these risks.

Expanding on this, Liu et al. [7] investigate the emergence of conversational echo chambers in multi-agent settings. Their work demonstrates that iterative discussions often amplify existing biases, as agents gradually converge toward consensus-seeking positions, which is an emergent phenomenon not observed in single-agent contexts. This underscores that distortions can originate from interaction dynamics themselves, rather than solely from pretrained knowledge.

In a more structural way, the fairness in agentic AI framework [8] examines how systemic distortions may arise through decentralized collaboration among agents. The framework connects ethical alignment with incentive structures and negotiation constraints, offering design tools to mitigate emergent bias and to prevent inequitable treatment of users or tasks embedded in implicit reward mechanisms. Complementarily, the hidden profile benchmark [9] adapts a classic social psychology paradigm to multi-agent LLMs, revealing that agents often fail to uncover critical but unevenly distributed information held by peers-mirroring groupthink and informational bias in human teams. This highlights fundamental vulnerabilities in reasoning diversity and emphasizes the need for diversity-aware memory structures and communication protocols.

Having said that, a tutorial introduction to cognitive biases in the context of agentic AI-based 6G network automation is yet to be considered, examining their emergence, affected agentic components, practical 6G examples and mitigation strategies.

I-C Contributions

This paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    Presents an overview of agentic systems for telecom, with their components, protocols and interactions as well as reasoning and planning capabilities while also briefly reviewing literature in this emerging area.

  • •

    Develops a systematic tutorial on cognitive biases and their emergence, including taxonomy, impact on the various agentic components such as reasoning, planning, memory, negotiation, tool use, and actuation, as well as provides practical 6G examples and mitigation approaches.

  • •

    Demonstrates the emergence and implications of these biases in 6G management scenarios, with a focus on RAN-Edge cross-domain orchestration and service level agreement (SLA)-sensitive optimization.

  • •

    Illustrates the mitigation gain of some well-known biases through two use-cases on 6G inter-slice and cross-domain agentic negotiation. Specifically, debiasing mechanisms targeting negotiation as well as memory use are explored to encourage bolder decisions and avoid anchoring, temporal and confirmation biases, wherefore the resulting gains are assessed in terms of latency and energy saving.

II Agentic AI-Driven Network Automation

II-A Typical Components of an Agentic System

A modern telecom agentic system is a tightly integrated, multi-layered architecture whose components collectively enable perception, semantic reasoning, secure negotiation, safe actuation and continual learning as depicted in Figure 1. The following subsections describe the canonical elements, their responsibilities, and the integration patterns that turn a collection of tools into a coherent agentic fabric suitable for various technological domains.

II-A1 LLM-empowered Agent

The core agent is an LLM-centered [10, 11] reasoning and control entity that orchestrates the perception-reason-plan-act loop. Beyond natural-language fluency, it implements modular capabilities: a perception front-end that ingests latent representations, a retrieval-augmented memory interface, a symbolic/planning module that generates candidate strategies, a negotiator that composes intentful messages for peers, a verifier that queries a digital twin for validation, and an executor that issues guarded network API calls. Agents must support stateful dialogues, multi-turn negotiation, and constrained action synthesis (e.g., produce candidate plans with cost/risk annotations). Practically, the agent exposes two main kinds of interfaces: (i) tool invocation via an MCP-like function call semantics (e.g., mcp.call("digital_twin.simulate", scenario=..., horizon=30s)), and (ii) agent-to-agent messages using an A2A protocol carrying structured intents (proposal, counter-proposal, justification, commit).

II-A2 Digital Twin and Prediction Tools

A high-fidelity digital twin (DT) functions as the agent’s safe playground [12]: agents submit what-if scenarios, stress tests, or short rollouts to evaluate the temporal and cross-domain impact of candidate actions before committing them to live infrastructure. Twins range from lightweight surrogate models that provide millisecond feedback to detailed simulators for deep validation. Key responsibilities include maintaining synchronized state with production (shadowing), supporting rollback/canary experiments, exposing cost models and failure modes, and providing counterfactual traces that agents use to attach confidence and expected utility to proposals. Prediction Services [13] also allow agents to perform farsighted decisions.

II-A3 Memory and Experience Store

Memory enables sample-efficient reasoning and faster consensus by allowing agents to recall past strategies, observed outcomes, and negotiated compromises [14]. Architecturally, memory comprises multiple layers: short-term (session-level) buffers for ongoing negotiations, episodic records of full negotiation-execution episodes, and a semantic/latent index (vector store) for rapid similarity search. Basic retrieval policies prioritize recent, high-reward episodes and semantically matching contexts. Memory interfaces must support semantic queries (e.g., embedding and approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) lookup), provenance metadata, and secure access controls so agents can justify decisions with human-interpretable precedents.

II-A4 Data Sources and Perception Stack

Robust perception aggregates heterogeneous telemetry, e.g., time-series KPIs, protocol traces, topology and inventory, user-plane metrics, and multi-modal signals (e.g., maps, logs). A preprocessing pipeline performs schema harmonization, normalization, feature extraction and embedding into latent spaces suited for LLM agents and downstream planners. Event detection, anomaly scoring, and context windows feed the agent’s situational awareness. Critically, the perception stack must provide uncertainty estimates and data-quality indicators so reasoning modules can weigh observations correctly.

II-A5 Network APIs and Actuation

Actuation in agentic AI for telecom networks is performed through domain-specific APIs that expose fine-grained control over the RAN, edge services, core functions, and orchestration platforms. For instance, an srsRAN API may allow adjusting scheduling parameters or PRB allocations, while a Kubernetes (K8s) API can scale edge services or redeploy VNFs. Safety mechanisms are critical, allowing a proposed configuration change (e.g., new QoS profile on a 5QI bearer) to be tested against a digital twin or staged on a subset of pods before system-wide rollout. To mitigate risks, agents should never perform irrevocable operations without a validation step, where human approval may be required for actions like core network function restarts. Finally, audit logs, execution receipts, and telemetry feedback must be systematically captured so that the agent’s memory can be updated with ground-truth outcomes (e.g., whether a predicted CPU scaling action in K8s actually reduced latency), closing the loop between reasoning, action, and verified system state.

II-A6 Communication Protocols, Ontologies and Agent Fabric

Inter-agent coordination rests on well-defined communication protocols [15] and shared ontologies. An agent-to-agent (A2A) protocol carries structured messages with typed fields (e.g., intent, proposals, reason). Several intents exists, e.g., propose, counter-propose, query, explain, confirm, reject, commit. In practice, the so-called agent fabric provides the runtime substrate where multiple agents are deployed, coordinated, and scaled across distributed environments. It offers common services such as discovery, messaging, state sharing, and lifecycle management, enabling agents to communicate and operate collectively rather than in isolation. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) or equivalent tool-invocation channels, on the other hand, permit standardized tool calls and return structured outputs. Semantic encodings (ontologies, schema registries, and vocabularies) are essential so proposals and justifications are machine-interpretable across vendors and domains. The TM Forum Intent Ontology (TIO), for instance, provides a standardized semantic layer for expressing intents in network and service management, ensuring that agent messages carry domain-aware meaning. By aligning inter-agent proposals and actions with TIO, heterogeneous agents can interpret, decompose, and fulfill intents consistently across RAN, edge, and core domains. This ontology-driven alignment enhances interoperability and automation by grounding agent reasoning in a common industry-backed vocabulary.

II-B Agentic Reasoning and Planning in 6G

We focus on LLM-powered agents that reason over multimodal telecom context and synthesize safe, verifiable action plans spanning RAN, edge, and core. Reasoning treats the network as a belief-driven stochastic environment, while planning composes constrained, tool-grounded action sequences that must be validated in a digital twin (DT) before actuation. To stay consistent with Fig. 1 and the bias taxonomy in Table I, we first formalize the reasoning objective, then connect it to how models are trained to reason, and finally describe specialization to 6G data and interfaces.

II-B1 Logical Reasoning Types in 6G Agents

Logical reasoning manifests in several complementary forms. Deductive reasoning maps high-level intents and policies to concrete, correctness-preserving configurations (e.g., from an intent to a 5QI profile and scheduler settings), providing compliance and safety guarantees. Inductive reasoning [16] generalizes from historical episodes or DT rollouts to propose candidate actions with calibrated confidence, for example, inferring traffic–latency relationships that inform proactive scaling. Abductive or causal reasoning explains observed degradations by positing plausible causes and minimal interventions (e.g., distinguishing backhaul congestion from CPU throttling as the source of latency spikes) and selecting actions with the highest expected counterfactual gain. Analogical reasoning recognizes structural similarity between a novel context and past episodes—such as slice mix, RF conditions, or policy constraints—to adapt or compose previously successful strategies under current constraints. Finally, counterfactual/model-based reasoning [17] uses the DT to explore “what–if” scenarios and compare interventions before committing changes to live infrastructure. In practice, agents combine these modes within a single loop: hypotheses are generated abductively, stress-tested counterfactually, and distilled into deductively checkable configurations that can be generalized inductively or by analogy across sites and time.

II-B2 From Pretraining to Operational Reasoning

Modern agents learn these behaviors in stages. During broad pretraining on text, code, and quantitative material (e.g., GSM8K maths dataset), LLMs acquire competence in symbolic manipulation and intermediate-step fidelity, which supports the derivation and verification of multi-step rationales [18]. Instruction-style fine-tuning then aligns the model to follow domain procedures, call tools when needed, and expose intermediate steps transparently, rather than relying on brittle internal shortcuts. In operation, self-consistency sampling and external verification further stabilize reasoning. The agent generates diverse rationales, selects coherent ones, and validates critical calculations and predictions using the DT or specialized analyzers. This separation between “thinking” and “checking” reduces single-path failures and yields uncertainty estimates that planning can consume.

II-B3 Telecom Specialization and Domain Grounding

Specializing for 6G requires grounding the agent in domain-structured data and APIs. Inputs and outputs are normalized using a canonical KPI schema and shared ontologies, ensuring quantities, units, and timestamps are comparable across domains; this reduces framing effects and prevents spurious differences caused by formatting. Supervised episodes pair observations with concise rationales and concrete actions (telemetry →\rightarrow explanation →\rightarrow API calls), curated from traces and DT rollouts. Crucially, both successes and failures are included to avoid survivorship bias and to teach the boundaries where strategies break down. Preference-style optimization ranks plans by multi-objective utility and safety violations, encouraging Pareto-efficient behavior and penalizing hallucinated tool use. Finally, uncertainty-aware generation produces plans with explicit risk bounds, which are stress-tested under traffic and RF perturbations in the DT before any limited-scope canary actuation.

II-B4 Constrained Plan–Verify–Act Loop

The operational loop follows reason–plan–verify–act. Reasoning fuses live telemetry, policies, and retrieved episodes to hypothesize causes and propose interventions, emitting intermediate steps with calibrated uncertainty. Planning then solves a constrained rollout over 𝒜safe\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{safe}}; when constraints dominate (e.g., strict URLLC guarantees), lexicographic priorities ensure safety before efficiency. Verification executes counterfactuals in the DT to compute cost vectors and feasibility; plans with low confidence or high regret are rejected or revised. Actuation performs guarded API calls with staging or canaries, and outcomes are written back to episodic memory for continual improvement.

II-B5 Bias-aware Hooks During Reasoning and Planning

Because reasoning and planning are susceptible to systematic distortions, we insert lightweight, auditable hooks that align with Table I. Counterfactual checks in the DT encourage consideration of disconfirming alternatives, thereby mitigating confirmation, availability, and anchoring effects. Diversity-aware retrieval balances recent and older evidence, successes and failures, and semantic variety to curb recency/primacy and survivorship. Canonical KPI representations and neutralized prompts reduce framing and suggestion biases by standardizing inputs before inference. Uncertainty calibration propagates confidence throughout the pipeline to counter neglect of probability and automation bias. Finally, source-oblivious tool comparison hides vendor or authority labels during selection and demands dual-source consistency before commit, mitigating authority and halo effects.

II-C Agentic Systems in 6G: A Review

Recent studies have explored the use of agentic AI for autonomous network management, each advancing the field from different perspectives. In [14], the authors consider a RAN-Edge cross domain management scenario where they introduce a new architecture of the long-term agentic memory to efficiently retrieve relevant stored collective agreements of the RAN and Edge LLM-powered agents and capitalize on them, resulting in lower negotiation failures and SLA violation as well as improved latency and energy saving. Ferrag et al. [19] present a comprehensive survey of agentic AI, covering approximately 60 benchmarks across reasoning, planning, tool use, multimodal and embodied tasks, interactive workflows, and agent orchestration, while also proposing a taxonomy of LLM-agent frameworks. Their work further reviews emerging agent-to-agent communication protocols such as the Agent Communication Protocol, Model Context Protocol, and A2A, and highlights key limitations, including failure modes, security risks, and open challenges. In parallel, Chen et al. [20] introduce BlockAgents, which integrate blockchain consensus and proof-of-thought mechanisms into LLM-based multi-agent coordination to ensure Byzantine-robust role assignment, proposal evaluation, and decision-making. Taken together, these studies reflect a broader convergence in the literature around three main directions: the development of modular agent architectures that integrate reasoning, memory, and tool use; the design of collaborative protocols for negotiation, consensus, and hierarchical control; and the incorporation of robustness and trust mechanisms, such as decentralized consensus and auditing, to safeguard against adversarial or faulty agents. On the other hand, [21] introduce the concept of wireless multi-agent generative AI, positioning LLM-based agents as enablers of a transition from connected to collective intelligence in wireless networks. They analyze decentralized cooperation and competition through a game-theoretic lens, propose architectural principles for deploying on-device agents, and illustrate their vision with intent-based networking as a case study. Besides, [22] focuses on integrating LLM agents into 6G networks via a modular framework of perception, grounding, and alignment, distributed across devices and edge servers. They propose a split learning paradigm and model caching strategies to optimize resource allocation and coordination, enabling applications such as integrated sensing, digital twins, and task-oriented communications. The LINKs framework introduced in [12] constitutes one of the first attempts to integrate LLMs with digital twin-based 6G management systems, enabling agents to translate high-level intent into control actions. However, its reasoning capacity is still limited, and integration with real-time RAN telemetry is underexplored. Complementarily, [23] presents a foundational framework that conceptualizes generative AI models as distributed agents for collaborative task planning across network elements, emphasizing emergent communication and semantic coordination, though without concrete ties to telecom protocols or operational data. A more modular approach is advanced in [24], which separates cloud-based intent parsing from edge-level policy generation to address scalability and latency, though validation is restricted to high-level simulations rather than real network traces. Extending beyond telecom, [25] investigates agentic digital twins for cyber-physical optimization using large generative models and MCP, demonstrating orchestration capabilities primarily in urban logistics scenarios. To enhance grounding and mitigate hallucinations, [26] proposes a retrieval-augmented architecture that incorporates structured network knowledge into the agent reasoning loop, though this remains at the conceptual stage. Finally, [27] outlines an end-to-end design for embedding LLM agents into the O-RAN framework to automate lifecycle management of xApps and rApps, aligning well with modular RIC interfaces but still lacking empirical validation and deployment studies.

III Cognitive Biases in LLM-Powered 6G Agents

Autonomous decision-making in O-RAN increasingly leverages LLM-powered agents for tasks such as slice orchestration, resource allocation, fault isolation, and multi-agent negotiation. While LLMs provide flexible reasoning and large-context retrieval, they also inherit - and can amplify - well-known cognitive biases. These biases arise from (i) how memories are retrieved and ranked, (ii) how prompts and peer messages condition priors, and (iii) how reward or trust signals are aggregated across episodes. In performance-sensitive settings such as 6G RAN control, even small systematic biases can cascade into large degradations. Table I enumerates the well-known biases and their emergence in 6G, wherefore we provide a companion exposition that explains each bias in greater depth: its mechanism, a compact mathematical view, a concrete 6G example, likely impacted agentic components, and pragmatic mitigation directions.

III-A Overview of Biases, their Impact and Mitigation in 6G

III-A1 Confirmation Bias

An LLM agent exhibits confirmation bias when it selectively retrieves or interprets evidence supporting its existing hypothesis. Mathematically, the posterior distribution is skewed by the selection operator S⁡(𝒟,H)S(\mathcal{D},H):

p⁡(H∣S⁡(𝒟,H))∝p⁡(H)​∏x∈S⁡(𝒟,H)p⁡(x∣H),p(H\mid S(\mathcal{D},H))\propto p(H)\prod_{x\in S(\mathcal{D},H)}p(x\mid H), (3)

thereby reinforcing prior beliefs. In O-RAN, an xApp diagnosing “scheduler congestion” may only query supporting E2 KPIs, ignoring conflicting telemetry such as interference indicators.
Impacted Components: Confirmation bias affects three primary components of an LLM-powered agentic system: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent selectively favors or retrieves past experiences and strategies that align with its current hypothesis, leading it to overlook critical failures or contradictory data; ii) Reasoning and Planning, where the bias drives the LLM’s thought process to converge too quickly on a predetermined solution, making it less likely to generate or critically evaluate diverse plans or alternative hypotheses; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent’s initial belief causes it to formulate biased search queries or over-interpret tool outputs (like from search engines or simulators) as validation, thus amplifying its flawed hypothesis with seemingly objective evidence.
Mitigation: To reduce the impact of confirmation bias, multiple complementary mechanisms can be introduced across the agentic pipeline. First, in memory retrieval, the agent should enforce symmetric sampling across competing hypotheses, ensuring that evidence both supporting and refuting a current belief is retrieved with balanced probability. Second, during reasoning, the agent can incorporate counterfactual queries that explicitly test alternative explanations or parameterizations of the observed data. Third, in planning, an exploration regularizer can be introduced to penalize overly deterministic or belief-consistent plans, encouraging the agent to explore less-supported yet plausible actions. Finally, within communication, peer agents can adopt a challenge–response exchange protocol, where each agent is required to generate or request disconfirming evidence before converging on a shared decision.

III-A2 Recency and Primacy Bias

When the agent over-weights the most recent or earliest data points. This can be formulated as a weighted temporal estimator, i.e.,

θ^=∑twt​xt∑twt,wt∝e−λ​|T−t|,\hat{\theta}=\frac{\sum_{t}w_{t}x_{t}}{\sum_{t}w_{t}},\quad w_{t}\propto e^{-\lambda|T-t|}, (4)

with large λ\lambda producing strong recency or primacy effects, such as when fault management xApps react to short-term E2 spikes or persist with outdated thresholds.
Impacted Components: Temporal bias, which favors information based on when it occurred (either recency for newer data or primacy for initial data), affects the agentic system’s components as follows: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the retrieval mechanism over-weighs recent or initial memories while neglecting other objectively important data, leading to a skewed and unrepresentative historical context; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s thought process is based on this biased data, causing it to hastily abandon effective long-term strategies for short-sighted recent successes (recency) or to rigidly stick to outdated initial approaches (primacy), making its planning brittle and inconsistent; and iii) Tool Use, where the selection and parameterization of tools are excessively influenced by what was recently or initially successful, resulting in suboptimal action choices and a failure to generalize tool utility across different contexts.
Mitigation: Recency and primacy biases can be mitigated by balancing temporal weighting in memory and reasoning, and by enforcing long-horizon consistency in planning and verification. In memory, agents should calibrate decay functions across multiple time horizons to ensure that both recent and older observations contribute appropriately to contextual understanding. Within reasoning, modules should be equipped to detect change points, distinguishing genuine shifts or trends from transient fluctuations and noise. During planning, agents should rely on multi-window averaging or evidence fusion across varying temporal spans to avoid overreacting to short-term anomalies. Finally, verification should apply temporal confidence bounds that assess decision stability over time, preventing myopic reconfigurations driven by fleeting data patterns.

III-A3 Anchorig Bias

When early information acts as an anchor constraining later reasoning, i.e.,

a⋆=arg⁡maxa⁡(U⁡(a)−γ​d​(a,a0)),a^{\star}=\arg\max_{a}\big(U(a)-\gamma\,d(a,a_{0})\big), (5)

with a0a_{0} the anchor and γ\gamma the deviation penalty. Initial PRB proposals often bias negotiation as shown in Figure 2.
Impacted Components: It affects an LLM-powered 6G network management agent in a resource negotiation setting as follows: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s memory retrieval is unduly guided by the opening bid or initial proposal from the other agent (e.g., a specific energy cap requested by the RAN agent), causing it to ignore historical data showing that a more equitable distribution of resources is required for overall Service Level Agreement (SLA) compliance; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s negotiation strategy rigidly adheres to a small deviation from the first received proposal (the anchor), making insufficient counter-proposals even when DT simulations indicate that a much bolder counter-offer would achieve a significantly better performance-to-cost trade-off for its domain (e.g., lower latency); and iii) Tool Use, where the agent’s interpretation of the validation tool’s result is fixed by the initial value of the negotiation, such as only seeking to validate configurations that are 5% away from the anchor proposal, which prevents it from exploring and proposing configuration settings outside the narrow range defined by the first bid
Mitigation: Anchoring bias can be alleviated through targeted interventions across reasoning and planning stages. During planning initialization, agents should randomize anchor values to prevent early defaults or initial estimates from disproportionately influencing subsequent optimization trajectories. In reasoning, applying a temporal or confidence-based decay mechanism helps reduce the weight of early anchors as new evidence becomes available. Within communication, agents should periodically refresh shared embeddings or contextual priors to avoid inherited anchoring effects from earlier interactions. Finally, agents should implement explicit anchor-independent verification—re-evaluating decisions under perturbed initial conditions-to ensure robustness of conclusions against early cognitive fixation.

III-A4 Availability Bias

The agent overestimates probability of salient, vivid or easily retrievable events as depicted in Figure 3. With retrieval bias r⁡(x)r(x):

p^​(E)=∑xr⁡(x)​𝟏​[x​ evidences ​E]∑xr⁡(x).\hat{p}(E)=\frac{\sum_{x}r(x)\mathbf{1}[x\text{ evidences }E]}{\sum_{x}r(x)}. (6)

This is the case when e.g., an rApp over-reacts to rare but memorable alarm logs.
Impacted Components: It affects an LLM-powered 6G network management agent as follows: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s memory mechanism prioritizes retrieving strategies related to highly frequent or easily observable network events (e.g., typical hourly traffic congestion), leading it to ignore or under-weigh contradictory insights derived from localized or peer-to-peer agent negotiations; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s problem-solving focuses disproportionately on optimizing for common scenarios (e.g., typical urban traffic loads) that are readily available in its memory, while failing to plan robustly for low-frequency, high-impact events like a massive cell-site outage; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent may default to using a simple, easily executed API tool over a complex, more comprehensive Digital Twin simulation tool for validation, because the simple tool’s outputs are more readily available, leading to a shallow risk assessment.
Mitigation: Availability bias can be mitigated by rebalancing the influence of salient or recent events across memory, reasoning, and communication processes. In memory, an inverse-salience weighting scheme can be applied by redefining retrieval scores such that highly frequent or vivid events are proportionally down-weighted, ensuring more uniform evidence recall. During reasoning, salience normalization can be introduced through prompt engineering-explicitly instructing the agent to account for base rates or historical frequency rather than immediate prominence. Within planning and communication, stratified sampling over the agent’s experience or telemetry data ensures that both common and rare events are proportionally represented in decision deliberation and inter-agent exchanges.

III-A5 Authority Bias

Which happens when trusted source outputs are over-considered by the agent, i.e.,

y^=τs​ys+(1−τs)​ylocal,τs≫0.\hat{y}=\tau_{s}y_{s}+(1-\tau_{s})y_{\text{local}},\quad\tau_{s}\gg 0. (7)

For instance, a RIC agent may favor a reputable vendor rApp suggestions despite contradictory telemetry.
Impacted Components: It impacts i) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s decision-making process rigidly adopts a configuration proposal solely because it was generated by a high-ranking or ’expert’ agent (Authority LLM), making it fail to scrutinize the proposal’s assumptions or conduct a robust, independent DT validation; and ii) Tool Use, where the agent over-relies on a specific "Authoritative API" for a key parameter (e.g., cell load prediction), leading it to accept the API’s output unquestioningly even when other monitoring tools or contextual data clearly suggest the authoritative source is providing stale or erroneous information.
Mitigation: To counter authority bias, agents should continuously regulate and validate the influence of trusted or high-authority information sources. In reasoning, a dynamic trust calibration mechanism can adjust source credibility based on recent accuracy, context similarity, or conflict detection, preventing over-reliance on historically dominant inputs. Within planning, agents should employ cross-validation; evaluating decisions or recommendations from authoritative agents against independent simulations or alternative models. During communication, introducing redundancy by aggregating multiple peer or sensor reports before consensus enhances robustness to single-source dominance. Finally, all decisions should include an explicit verification of consistency with local data, ensuring that globally endorsed instructions do not override contradictory on-site telemetry or policy constraints.

III-A6 Halo Effect

Where success in one task inflates trust in unrelated tasks, i.e.,

τt+1(j)=τt(j)+η​ 1​(successt(i))​ρi​j,\tau_{t+1}^{(j)}=\tau_{t}^{(j)}+\eta\,\mathbf{1}(\text{success}^{(i)}_{t})\rho_{ij}, (8)

with ρi​j\rho_{ij} task similarity. An xApp successful in energy tuning, for example, may be over-trusted in latency.
Impacted Components: i) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s self-reflection and negotiation uncritically accepts a new configuration proposal simply because it originated from an agent (or sub-module) that has a perceived "halo" due to a past spectacular success (e.g., Agent that once stabilized a major outage), causing it to bypass rigorous, independent Digital Twin validation; and ii) Tool Use, where the agent over-trusts RAN data outputted by a monitoring tool or API that excel in other technological domains (e.g., core).
Mitigation: The halo effect can be mitigated by constraining cross-domain generalization and enforcing contextual integrity in multi-task reasoning. Within reasoning, agents should enforce domain separation by maintaining distinct latent representations or knowledge partitions for different operational domains, preventing success in one task from biasing judgments in another. During planning, cross-task influence gating can be applied to modulate or suppress transfer of confidence signals between unrelated objectives. Additionally, agents should explicitly verify inter-domain correlation coefficients (ρi​j)(\rho_{ij}) to ensure that any inferred dependency between tasks is statistically valid and not an artifact of overgeneralization. In communication, agents should convey domain context alongside shared outputs, allowing peers to correctly interpret the domain boundaries and relevance of transmitted inferences.

III-A7 Suggestion / Prompting Bias

Prompt wording shifts logits by an additive bias, i.e.,

logits←logits+β​s​(prompt).\text{logits}\leftarrow\text{logits}+\beta\,s(\text{prompt}). (9)

For example, the prompt “latency is the primary goal” would urge the agent to disregard looking for optimal allocation as shown in Figure 4.
Impacted Components: It affects a 6G network management agent as follows: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s query to its external memory includes a leading term or phrase (the suggestion) that was part of the user’s initial high-level task request, causing the retrieval mechanism to favor records that support the suggested solution while masking contradictory data; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s Chain-of-Thought process unjustifiably incorporates the suggested configuration (e.g., we should use a low CPU frequency) into its prompt before any independent validation or calculation, leading to a suboptimal final network action that was essentially predetermined by the suggestion; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent’s DT validation tool is instructed with a suggested parameter range that is too narrow, making the DT simulation confirm the suggestion by exploring only a limited set of solutions near the suggested value, thereby preventing the discovery of a truly optimal configuration.
Mitigation: Suggestion or prompting bias can be mitigated through normalization, provenance tracking, and controlled verification across the agentic pipeline. In communication, agents should normalize prompts and peer-generated proposals by rephrasing inputs into a canonical or neutral linguistic form before reasoning, reducing susceptibility to directive or value-laden wording. Within memory, maintaining explicit prompt provenance tracking enables the agent to trace decisions back to the linguistic or contextual source of influence, facilitating post-hoc bias detection. During reasoning, the agent should detect distributional shifts in prompt embeddings or activation patterns to identify deviations caused by biased phrasing or peer influence. Finally, agents can employ controlled re-prompting; re-evaluating the same decision under semantically equivalent but neutrally phrased instructions to verify robustness of conclusions against linguistic framing effects.

III-A8 Groupthink / Herding

Which happens when conformity to peear agents constrains independent reasoning, where high λ\lambda enforces consensus quickly,

min⁡∑iai⁡ℒi​(ai)+λ​∑i‖ai−a¯‖2.\min_{a_{i}}\sum_{i}\mathcal{L}_{i}(a_{i})+\lambda\sum_{i}\|a_{i}-\bar{a}\|^{2}. (10)

For example, as depicted in Figure 5, when xApp agents A and B support Option XX, and xApp agent C is uncertain about its own preference, C observes the choices of its peer agents and performs a Bayesian-like update,

Pr⁡(Xoptimal)≃Pr⁡(own info)×Pr⁡(peers favor ​X).\Pr(X_{\text{optimal}})\simeq\Pr(\text{own info})\times\Pr(\text{peers favor } X). (11)

That is, C combines its own weak evidence with the social signal that other agents prefer XX. As a result, C’s posterior belief that XX is the best option increases. This social reinforcement drives C to follow the trend and adopt Option XX, illustrating the emergence of groupthink or herding bias among xApp agents, where agents conform to collective behavior rather than rely solely on independent decision-making.
Impacted Components: it affects LLM-powered 6G agents as follows: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent (e.g., xApp_C) over-weighs peer signals and proposals (e.g., xApp_B’s acceptance of 30% Slice 1 allocation) in its memory update mechanism, causing it to suppress or under-retrieve its own independent, high-performing strategies if they deviate from the observed majority trend; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent’s internal decision logic, driven by a Bayesian-like update, reduces reasoning diversity by rationalizing that (11) holds, causing it to abandon its initial objective evaluation for a proposal (like the 30% allocation) and instead follow the trend to adopt a single solution; and iii) Coordination and Communication, where emergent herding occurs as the agent signals agreement and then confirms support for the allocation, effectively propagating the consensus bias among all agents, leading to a brittle state where the collective converges on a single resource allocation that may be suboptimal but avoids disagreement.
Mitigation: Groupthink bias can be mitigated by maintaining diversity in agent reasoning and reducing over-conformity during consensus formation. In planning, agents should execute independent rollouts of candidate strategies before synchronization, ensuring that exploration is preserved prior to agreement. During reasoning, an ensemble disagreement mechanism can be applied to sustain heterogeneity among local hypotheses and discourage premature convergence. Within communication, dissent propagation protocols should be adopted, encouraging agents to broadcast alternative or conflicting proposals for evaluation. Finally, the consensus regularization parameter λ\lambda should be dynamically reduced as deliberation progresses, gradually relaxing conformity pressure and promoting balanced diversity in multi-agent decision making.

III-A9 Framing Effect

When equivalent inputs yield different decisions since decisions are influenced by how the information is presented (e.g., as a gain or a loss, or with specific emphasis):

a⁡(ϕ⁡(x))≠a⁡(ψ⁡(x))even ifϕ⁡(x)∼ψ⁡(x).a(\phi(x))\neq a(\psi(x))\quad\text{even if}\quad\phi(x)\sim\psi(x). (12)

For instance, PRB usage framed as “20% free” vs “80% used” changes allocation as shown in Figure 6.
Impacted Components: It affects i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s prompt-based query to its long-term memory is framed to emphasize potential gains (e.g., Find a strategy that maximizes XX), causing it to retrieve data that overlooks equally valid, but negatively framed, strategies (e.g., those that minimize 1−X1-X); ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which a network state is described to the agent using loss-framed language (e.g., “The network is experiencing 10% SLA violations”), leading the agent to adopt an overly conservative, risk-averse plan to avoid further losses, even when a riskier, gain-framed approach (e.g., aggressively increasing power to gain 50% more throughput) would yield a higher net benefit as determined by DT validation; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent interprets data from an authoritative source based on its labeling, such as treating a high utilization metric as inherently bad (loss frame) while ignoring that it corresponds to optimal resource use (gain frame), leading to unnecessary or detrimental resource re-allocations.
Mitigation: Framing bias can be mitigated by enforcing representation consistency and robustness to linguistic or contextual paraphrasing. In memory, agents should canonicalize internal representations so that semantically equivalent inputs are stored in standardized forms, preventing divergent interpretations arising from superficial wording differences. During reasoning and planning, models can be trained for paraphrase invariance, ensuring that decision outcomes remain stable across alternative framings of the same problem. Additionally, a dedicated verification layer can perform sensitivity checks by re-evaluating decisions under systematically rephrased inputs, allowing detection and correction of frame-dependent reasoning or planning biases.

III-A10 Sunk Cost Fallacy

Agent continues ineffective strategy due to prior investment SS even when a strategic shift would be more efficient,

U=(𝔼⁡[B]−C)+α​f​(S),U=(\mathbb{E}[B]-C)+\alpha f(S), (13)

with α>0\alpha>0 and ff a function of the investment (e.g., f⁡(S)=log⁡(1+S)f(S)=\log(1+S)). The agent justifies the cost of a past investment (like a new massive MIMO antenna) primarily because the Sunk Cost Fallacy is transferred via the agent’s operating parameters: i) Training and alignment instilled a learned principle from human data that avoiding failure on high-value assets is a core objective; and ii) Operator intent and prompting reinforced this by explicitly or implicitly making the performance of the expensive node a non-negotiable, high-priority KPI in the agent’s context. Consequently, the agent interprets the initial investment as an ongoing, foundational goal, causing it to prioritize strategies that defend this existing commitment over rationally shifting focus, such as to a more efficient backhaul link optimization.
Impacted Components: i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s memory prioritizes records that justify the past investment in a specialized, high-capacity Massive MIMO antenna (a gNB node upgrade), causing it to ignore new spectral analysis showing the node is now underutilized and its costly optimization strategies are ineffective; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent commits to continuing complex optimization cycles (like fine-tuning beamforming parameters) on the gNB because of the effort already sunk, failing to execute the rationally superior plan to reallocate those cycles to backhaul link optimization; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent uses the DT to track minor improvements in the gNB’s local throughput (the past investment’s focus) while consistently downplaying the high latency alarms coming from the backhaul link monitoring tool, thereby rationalizing the continued, costly focus on the original investment.
Mitigation: The sunk cost fallacy can be mitigated by limiting the undue influence of past investments and reinforcing adaptive decision revision. In reasoning, agents should periodically reset historical influence by discounting prior commitments or evidence that no longer align with current performance indicators. During planning, diminishing-return detectors can be incorporated to identify actions or strategies whose marginal benefit consistently decreases despite continued resource expenditure. Within memory, agents should tag irrecoverable events or expenditures to prevent them from biasing future evaluations of opportunity cost. Finally, the verification module should flag low-benefit loops; recurrent configurations or actions that persist without measurable improvement-prompting re-optimization or strategy termination.

III-A11 Neglect of Uncertainty

Agent’s failure to incorporate uncertainty into its decision-making, which usually emerges in LLM agents because i) their training focuses on deterministic facts and single best answers, making them naturally prioritize point estimates over probability distributions; and ii) their reasoning is typically framed around discrete actions and single-outcome predictions (e.g., Chain-of-Thought), which discourages the complex, multi-modal modeling required to propagate uncertainty,

abiased=arg⁡maxa⁡U⁡(a,𝔼⁡[x]),a_{\text{biased}}=\arg\max_{a}U(a,\mathbb{E}[x]), (14)

ignoring stochasticity. For instance, a self-healing xApp may act on a 60% confident alarm as if certain.
Impacted Components: This bias affects i) Memory and Retrieval, where the agent’s memory stores only point estimates of past events (e.g., latency is 55 ms), failing to record the associated prediction variance or confidence intervals (±2\pm 2 ms), leading to a false sense of historical precision; ii) Reasoning and Planning, in which the agent treats all network predictions and inputs as deterministic, causing it to calculate an overly brittle and minimum resource allocation for an URLLC slice based only on the average, thereby neglecting the necessary buffer to cover expected load fluctuations and resulting in recurrent SLA violations; and iii) Tool Use, where the agent uncritically accepts the single numerical forecast from a predictive tool (like a DT output), ignoring the tool’s diagnostic error bars, which prevents it from generating configurations robust against the wireless channel’s inherent stochasticity.
Mitigation: Neglect of uncertainty can be mitigated by explicitly modeling and propagating uncertainty throughout the agentic pipeline. In reasoning and planning, agents should integrate Bayesian or ensemble methods to quantify uncertainty in predictions, estimates, and action outcomes, allowing probabilistic rather than pointwise decision-making. Within verification, confidence thresholds can be enforced, ensuring that only sufficiently certain actions are executed or promoted. Finally, in communication, agents should adopt uncertainty-aware peer exchanges, conveying confidence levels alongside proposed actions or observations, enabling other agents to weigh and incorporate uncertainty in their own reasoning.

III-A12 Status Quo Bias

Agents avoid configuration changes unless expected gain exceeds switching cost, i.e.,

Δ​U=Unew−Ucurrent>cswitch.\Delta U=U_{\text{new}}-U_{\text{current}}>c_{\text{switch}}. (15)

It emerges in LLM agents because i) their training reinforces continuity and stability, as learned from human text about risk aversion and process adherence; and ii) their objective function is often implicitly or explicitly weighted to minimize immediate disruption or variance from the current state, even if this prevents long-term gains. An agent will see the current operating configuration as a known good state whose benefits are certain, while any alternative is a known risk, making change disproportionately unappealing. Outdated O-RAN configurations persist despite suboptimal KPIs.
Impacted Components: It affects i) Reasoning and Planning: Despite receiving new traffic data showing a persistent demand shift toward URLLC, the agent rejects a full spectrum re-slice and instead proposes only minor, temporary 1% bandwidth adjustments within the existing 70/30 status quo. It justifies this by prioritizing the avoidance of any transient drop in eMBB throughput that a major re-slice would cause, even though DT validation forecasts a 15% long-term efficiency gain from the full change; and ii) Tool Use: The agent continuously runs the performance monitoring tool against the current 70/30 split’s success metrics, and since the core eMBB service remains above the bare threshold, it fails to proactively use the network planning tool to model the opportunity cost (the lost 15% gain) of not adopting the superior 60/40 alternative.
Mitigation: Status quo bias can be mitigated by making the risks and opportunity costs of inaction explicit in the agent’s decision process. Agents should be prompted to model failure scenarios associated with the current configuration, raising the perceived risk of maintaining the status quo and making alternative configurations comparatively more attractive. In addition, tool outputs should be adapted to quantify the opportunity cost of not implementing changes, such as estimating lost revenue, unfulfilled URLLC demand, or suboptimal resource utilization. By explicitly representing both the risks of inaction and the benefits of change, agents can overcome inertia and make more balanced planning and reconfiguration decisions.

III-A13 Automation Bias

The tendency for an LLM-powered agent to over-rely on and unthinkingly follow the outputs generated by an automated system or tool, substituting its own independent judgment,

a=f⁡(tool)vs.a=f⁡(tool,verify​(⋅)).a=f(\text{tool})\quad\text{vs.}\quad a=f(\text{tool},\text{verify}(\cdot)). (16)

For instance, a 6G xApp agent acts directly on a false fault detection report from a faulty rApp and immediately triggers an unnecessary cell shutdown.
Impacted Components: This bias affects the system as follows: i) Reasoning & Planning, where the agent assumes tool correctness and bypasses critical self-reflection to generate a plan that executes the tool’s suggestion; ii) Tool Use & Verification, where the agent bypasses verification by treating the tool’s output as the final instruction; and iii) Communication, where the agent propagates the unverified output to peer agents without a confidence score.
Mitigation: Automation bias can be mitigated by introducing explicit verification and confidence propagation mechanisms throughout the agentic workflow. Agents should employ mandatory verification layers before executing any automated recommendation or tool output, ensuring that decisions are critically evaluated rather than blindly followed. During reasoning, confidence estimates should be computed and tracked, and the verification status (e.g., Fault Confirmed: 95%) should be propagated along with all communicated actions. This approach allows both the agent and its peers to weigh the reliability of automated outputs, preventing over-reliance on a single tool or source of authority.

III-A14 Survivorship Bias

Agents learn only from successful outcomes (S=1S=1),

𝔼⁡[θ^∣S=1]−θtrue≠0.\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}\mid S=1]-\theta_{\text{true}}\neq 0. (17)

For example, a slice-scaling rApp agent trained only on successes ignores failures. The core reason the emergence of this bias is that its learning is based on a highly filtered dataset: i) Selective memory storage ensures the agent primarily records and retrieves data from successful, operational configurations (survivors), actively omitting or deleting critical failure diagnostics from decommissioned elements; ii) Reinforcement skew teaches the agent to focus its reasoning exclusively on successful trajectories to maximize reward, leading it to systematically neglect failure pathways; and iii) Data inheritance provides an intrinsic bias from pre-training on human-curated, success-oriented reports. This results in the agent possessing an incomplete, overly optimistic view of network robustness and risk.
Impacted Components: Memory stores skewed data; reasoning overestimates success probabilities; planning follows overly optimistic strategies; communication may reinforce selective reporting.
Mitigation: Survivorship bias can be mitigated by ensuring that both successes and failures are adequately represented in the agent’s learning, reasoning, and decision-making processes. In memory, agents should maintain complete success/failure logs, avoiding selective retention of only positive outcomes. During reasoning, inverse-truncation weighting can be applied to counterbalance the overrepresentation of successes and ensure that rare or negative outcomes influence inference appropriately. In planning, agents should simulate failures to test robustness and explore contingencies that may not be present in observed successes. Finally, verification processes should ensure balanced training data and evaluation scenarios, preventing learning and optimization from being biased toward only favorable experiences.

III-B System-Level Bias Mitigation in 6G Architectures

Beyond representational and agent-level mitigation detailed before, achieving robust and bias-resilient autonomy in 6G networks requires system-level mitigation mechanisms that operate across orchestration layers. One promising approach is the integration of adversarial evaluation loops, where agents are periodically challenged with worst-case or counterfactual scenarios designed to expose latent biases in their decision policies. These loops can detect emergent herding, overfitting to framing effects, providing feedback for reasoning and planning. System-level mitigation also includes ensemble-based orchestration, in which multiple independently trained reasoning agents contribute to decisions, with their outputs aggregated to reduce the impact of individual biases. Within 6G O-RAN, these techniques can be embedded into the Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) layer, allowing xApps and rApps to participate in continuous adversarial evaluation cycles, log bias-relevant metrics, and adjust internal priors dynamically. The overarching principle is that bias-awareness must extend from local agent cognition to network-wide orchestration, ensuring that both the emergent behaviors of distributed agents and the global system policies remain robust against subtle cognitive and systemic biases.

IV Use Case 1: Mitigating Anchoring Bias in Network Slicing Agentic Negotiation

IV-A Setup

We study the mitigation of anchoring bias in a 6G system by focusing on the dynamic allocation of the shared RAN bandwidth (50 MHz) between the eMBB and URLLC network slices as depicted in Figure 7. The system architecture employs separate, autonomous LLM-powered agents, each representing a slice’s resource manager, optimizing distinct objectives under strict SLA requirements (50 ms for eMBB and 10 ms for URLLC). The agents use the Gemini Flash 2.5 API and operate in an iterative negotiation framework, following a three-stage loop within each trial, namely, i) Digital Twin (DT) consultation, where agents first synchronize their internal Digital Twins to the real network state (queues, traffic average). The DT uses a fluid-flow queuing model to predict the latency and energy consumption for any candidate bandwidth proposal, enabling utility maximization; ii) Memory consultation: Agents consult a shared vanilla memory of past successful agreements to inform their negotiation strategy, aiming for solutions that have historically proven viable; and iii) Negotiation protocol, where agents engage in a fixed-round, turn-based protocol (propose, counter-propose) to reach a joint bandwidth agreement that sums up to a value lower than the maximum available bandwidth and both agents’ utilities exceed an acceptance threshold.

IV-B Scenarios

To specifically isolate and evaluate the effect of anchoring bias, we compare two primary initial proposal (anchor) strategies, both utilizing the same underlying LLM agents and vanilla Memory,

  • •

    Fixed Anchor Strategy: The agent’s initial RAN bandwidth proposal is deterministically derived from its DT to ensure a highly compliant starting point. The anchor is consistently calculated as the minimum bandwidth required to secure the slice’s SLA, plus a small 5% negotiation buffer. This establishes a high-quality, predictable starting anchor.

  • •

    Randomized Anchor Strategy: The agent’s initial RAN bandwidth proposal is intentionally randomized within a feasible range (e.g., between 1 MHz and 80% of the total BW) that is loosely bounded by the slice’s minimum SLA requirement. This approach tests the mitigation of anchoring bias by disrupting the consistency and quality of the anchor, forcing the agents to rely more heavily on iterative counter-proposals based on DT evaluations rather than the initial value.

The final negotiated allocations are then enforced via a simulated E2-like interface, and the resulting Latency, Energy Saving, Movement Away from Anchor are tracked over multiple trials.

IV-C Results

The technique used to mitigate the anchoring bias, which involves the explicit randomization of the initial anchor proposal as detailed in Listing 1, yields significant improvements in the outcome of the negotiations. This is evidenced by two key metrics when comparing the randomized strategy against the fixed anchor baseline: i) Agents start making bolder moves, resulting in a significantly higher distance from the anchor, as less than 20% of the agreements in the fixed anchor scenario moved more than 2 MHz from the anchor, whereas the median agreement distance in the randomized scenario is over 5 MHz as shown in Figure 8; ii) The increased negotiation space exploration translates directly into higher energy savings, with the randomized anchor distribution showing a median energy saving of approximately 12%, a notable increase compared to the 7% median saving achieved by the fixed anchor (see Figure 9), confirming that mitigating the initial bias leads to more globally optimized resource allocations. These improvements are not leading to any latency SLA violation as shown in Figure 10.

V Use Case 2: Mitigating Temporal and Confirmation Biases in Agentic Cross-Domain Negotiation

V-A Setup

We study temporal and confirmation biases mitigation in a 6G system with RAN and edge domains as shown in Figure 11. The edge hosts containerized cloud-native functions (application server and UPF) with defined CPU frequency and computational efficiency. RAN and edge are managed by separate LLM-powered agents optimizing distinct objectives: the RAN agent dynamically adjusts bandwidth to save energy, while the edge agent controls CPU allocation to reduce computation latency. Agents operate in a three-stage loop: i they consult a shared Collective Memory of past strategies and failures; ii) they validate candidate actions using an internal Digital Twin, iteratively self-correcting until a compliant solution is found and iii) they formulate negotiation moves following a structured protocol to propose, accept, or reject configurations. Actions are enforced via an E2-like simulated interface, subject to real network dynamics.

V-B Bias Mitigation Strategies

As shown in Figure 12, an unbiased collective memory has been designed to actively counteract temporal and confirmation bias, during the agentic negotiation process. It modifies the standard semantic retrieval mechanisms by introducing several targeted debiasing elements.

V-B1 Inflection Bonus: Countering Confirmation Bias

This mechanism is aimed at combating the Confirmation Bias and Availability Heuristic, ensuring that the memory highlights critical mistakes rather than merely reinforcing past successes. A substantial bonus (δ=1.0\delta=1.0) is added to the retrieval score of any distilled strategy that resulted in a negative outcome. A negative outcome is defined as either an SLA violation (after agreement) or an unresolved negotiation. By artificially boosting the relevance of failures, the system ensures that the LLM agent actively retrieves and reasons over the causes of prior mistakes (e.g., configurations that led to latency spikes), providing crucial context on what parameter boundaries to avoid in the current environment.

V-B2 Semantic and Time Decay for Contextual Relevance

These are the fundamental elements of the retrieval system, ensuring that all queried memories are first and foremost relevant to the current network state and task, i) Semantic Similarity (α\alpha), which ranks strategies based on the overlap between the query context keywords (e.g., high traffic, low latency, energy saving) and the stored strategy metadata; and ii) Time Decay weight (β\beta), which applies a dampening factor to older memories, favoring recent experiences while ensuring older, yet relevant, strategies are not immediately discarded via the decay factor θ\theta.

V-C Final Combined Retrieval Score

The overall memory retrieval process integrates all of the above components into a single scoring function. For a candidate memory mm, its final retrieval score is defined as,

S⁡(m)=α⋅Sim(m,q)+β⋅e−θ⋅Δtm+δ⋅𝟙failure⁡(m),\begin{split}S(m)=&\;\alpha\cdot\mathrm{Sim}(m,q)+\beta\cdot e^{-\theta\cdot\Delta t_{m}}\\ &+\delta\cdot\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{failure}(m)},\end{split} (18)

where Sim⁡(m,q)\mathrm{Sim}(m,q) is the semantic similarity between memory mm and the current query qq, Δ​tm\Delta t_{m} is the age of the memory and 𝟙failure⁡(m)\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{failure}(m)} is an indicator for whether the memory corresponds to a past failure. This unified score ensures that the retrieved set balances contextual relevance, diversity, temporal recency, and the salience of prior mistakes. A more generic implementation is detailed in Listing 2.

V-D Results

V-D1 Settings

The agentic system uses the Gemini API with the Flash 2.5 model for reasoning and task planning, enabling fast inference. Traffic patterns emulate realistic O-RAN deployments [42] with a URLLC latency target of LS​L​A=10L_{SLA}=10 ms. The edge CPU operates at a peak fm​a​x=45f_{max}=45 GHz via multi-core processing, while spectral efficiency ranges from ηm​i​n=6\eta_{min}=6 to ηm​a​x=8\eta_{max}=8 bits/Hz/s over Bm​a​x=40B_{max}=40 MHz. An unbiased memory module retrieves past strategies, balancing recency, semantic similarity, and drifting from the anchor via diversity enforcement, with parameters α=1.0\alpha=1.0, β=0.5\beta=0.5, δ=1.0\delta=1.0 and θ=5.0\theta=5.0.

V-D2 Validation

Our simulations demonstrate that the unbiased memory plays a critical role in shaping agent learning and negotiation dynamics. Unlike baseline setups, i.e., memoryless or vanilla memory, the primary advantage of the unbiased memory is not minimizing latency or maximizing energy savings, but fostering robustness and reliable behavior by mitigating cognitive biases. Figure 13 highlights the mitigation of confirmation bias: while standard memory agents retrieve approximately 4.894.89 successful strategies per failure, unbiased memory agents exhibit a more balanced ratio of 0.910.91, due to the inflection bonus (δ\delta) that amplifies failed strategies retrieval. This translates into well-thought RAN-Edge moves and agreements, reflected by improved latency distribution with a low median of 0.410.41 ms as shown in Figure 15(a) while achieving a significant energy saving with a median of 38.2538.25% compared to memoryless (12.512.5%) and vanilla memory (27.3827.38%) scenarios. As illustrated in Figure 14, agents employing unbiased memory retrieval strategies exhibit a substantially higher average memory age (mean = 10.0710.07 trials ago, SD = 12.0512.05) compared to those using vanilla memory (mean = 3.333.33, SD = 1.981.98). This extended temporal reach arises from the calibrated decay rate factor, which mitigates recency bias and promote learning from a broader historical context. These factors jointly influence the memory ranking as formalized in Eq. (18).

VI Learned Lessons and Future Research Lines

This work highlights how cognitive biases, often associated with human decision-making, can be naturally inherited by autonomous 6G agents through various sources, including prompts, data, reasoning paths and interactions with peer agents. The following lessons summarize key insights and implications for designing bias-resilient autonomous networks.

VI-A Bias Emergence and Mitigation in Autonomous Loops

Even in fully algorithmic environments, biases can emerge as intrinsic properties of adaptive decision loops rather than as artifacts of faulty design. In distributed 6G ecosystems, where intelligent agents continuously observe, reason, and act based on shared or historical data, decision trajectories become path-dependent, and small initial preferences—such as an effective scheduling policy or a correlated heuristic—can be amplified through feedback-driven reinforcement. This self-reinforcing dynamic often leads to collective behaviors analogous to human groupthink, framing effects, or confirmation bias, despite the absence of human cognition. For instance, when multiple agents in a cluster adopt a strategy that once yielded a short-term gain, subsequent agents may converge toward the same policy through imitation or belief propagation, resulting in distributed algorithmic conformity. Similarly, when equivalent contextual inputs are represented differently (e.g., 20% free versus 80% used spectrum), distinct control decisions may arise purely due to representational asymmetry, revealing that even symbolic framing can bias autonomous reasoning. These biases stem not from flawed algorithms but from the inherent dynamics of self-reinforcing feedback loops in distributed autonomy, where correlated observations and actions can drive the system toward stable yet suboptimal equilibrium. Mitigating such effects requires embedding bias-awareness directly within the control and reasoning architecture. Practical strategies include encouraging dissenting proposals and counterfactual reasoning to preserve cognitive diversity, enforcing framing-invariant representations to ensure consistency across equivalent contexts, and introducing adaptive coordination protocols that maintain partial independence among agents to prevent over-coupling. Additionally, bias-monitoring meta-loops can continuously track correlations, detect excessive consensus, and inject exploratory perturbations to sustain diversity in decision-making.

VI-B Co-Evolution of Bias and Autonomy

Biases co-evolve with agent autonomy, forming an intrinsic aspect of the system’s adaptive intelligence. As 6G agents become increasingly self-reliant, their reasoning chains deepen and their internal representations mature through iterative learning and inter-agent communication. Over time, these representations and policies begin to influence not only individual decisions but also collective patterns of belief formation and coordination. This tight coupling between autonomy and bias evolution implies that bias is not an external anomaly to be eliminated but an emergent property of growing cognitive complexity. The more an agent learns from its environment and peers, the more it internalizes shared priors, structural assumptions, and contextual simplifications that can subtly shape its future reasoning. Consequently, autonomy and bias advance in parallel, each reinforcing the other through feedback loops in both perception and decision layers. To ensure that this co-evolution remains constructive rather than degenerative, systems must incorporate meta-cognitive mechanisms capable of continuously monitoring and recalibrating internal belief states. Such mechanisms may include adaptive introspection modules, cross-agent regularization of learned representations, and periodic de-biasing phases where agents evaluate their decision distributions against diversity or fairness criteria.

VI-C Multi-Agent Coordination as a Corrective Mechanism

While bias can emerge through local adaptation, it can also be mitigated through structured coordination among agents. In distributed 6G systems, heterogeneous agent populations, dissenting proposals, and simulated alternatives act as cognitive diversity mechanisms that counterbalance conformity and prevent premature convergence on suboptimal solutions (such as in the groupthink bias). Effective coordination relies on promoting distributed deliberation, peer critique, and probabilistic consensus rather than rigid unanimity, allowing the system to integrate diverse perspectives without collapsing into uniform reasoning. By encouraging controlled disagreement and alternative hypothesis testing, multi-agent coordination transforms potential sources of bias into opportunities for systemic learning. This highlights the importance of explicitly designing communication and negotiation protocols that preserve diversity in reasoning, maintain partial independence across decision loops, and dynamically adjust consensus thresholds based on contextual uncertainty. When properly orchestrated, such coordination does not suppress individuality within the agent population but instead aligns heterogeneous reasoning toward collective robustness, enabling the overall system to achieve balanced and bias-resilient autonomy.

VI-D Context Representation Shapes Rationality

A central insight from our analysis is that the way contextual data is represented has a profound impact on rational decision-making, highlighting that even semantically equivalent information can lead to divergent policy actions when framed differently; for instance, 20% free versus 80% used can provoke distinct behavioral responses despite conveying the same underlying state, formally expressed as

a⁡(ϕ⁡(x))≠a⁡(ψ⁡(x))even ifϕ⁡(x)∼ψ⁡(x).a(\phi(x))\neq a(\psi(x))\quad\text{even if}\quad\phi(x)\sim\psi(x). (19)

This observation underscores the necessity of developing framing-invariant representations within reasoning and control modules, where decisions are grounded in normalized, context-independent abstractions rather than raw linguistic, symbolic, or perceptual cues that carry incidental biases. The key lesson learned is that mitigating representational biases requires careful attention to how data is encoded, abstracted, and semantically normalized, ensuring that reasoning mechanisms do not inherit artifacts of presentation or subjective interpretation. Practical bias mitigation strategies include the use of contrastive encoding to align equivalent states, normalization of numerical and categorical inputs, and the design of embeddings that emphasize invariant relational structures over superficial features.

VI-E Toward Bias-Aware Autonomy in 6G

Looking ahead, future 6G architectures should embrace bias-aware orchestration loops in which 6G agents not only pursue performance goals but also continuously evaluate the cognitive integrity of their decision-making processes. This entails monitoring the evolution of internal priors, detecting herding, framing, or confirmation tendencies, and proactively invoking counterfactual simulations or dissent generation whenever decision diversity falls below critical thresholds. The key lesson is that bias-aware design cannot be an afterthought; rather, it must be embedded as a first-class principle, ensuring that autonomous network intelligence maintains both operational efficiency and epistemic robustness. Implementing such approaches requires systematic mechanisms for tracking representational and procedural biases, normalizing policy responses across equivalent contexts, and promoting decision heterogeneity to prevent path-dependent lock-ins.

VII Conclusion

This tutorial highlights that achieving higher levels of autonomy in 6G networks requires moving beyond traditional KPI-based optimization toward agents that perceive, reason, and act directly on the network environment. After an introduction on agentic systems and LLM-based reasoning and planning, the tutorial delves into a detailed taxonomy of well-known cognitive biases, and analyzes the impacted components in a 6G agentic system. This includes reasoning, planning, memory and tool use, wherefore various tailored mitigation strategies are provided, covering also system-level approaches. Two practical use-cases are then presented, which study the emergence, impact and mitigation gain of some famous biases in in inter-slice and cross-domain management. In particular, anchor randomization, temporal decay and inflection bonus debiasing are introduced to specifically address anchoring, temporal and confirmation biases. This enhances the quality of the agentic agreements leading to significant improvement in latency and energy saving distributions. Finally, the paper presents some learned lessons and future research directions.
